citation: Ding W, Li B, Ma X (2026). Effects of flywheel resistance training on jump, sprint, and change-of-direction performance in basketball players: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Frontiers in Physiology.
population: 119 basketball players (collegiate, youth, amateur, professional; male and female) across 7 randomized controlled trials
intervention: Flywheel resistance training (4-8 weeks, 1-2 sessions/week) using lower-body multi-joint exercises (squat, half squat, Romanian deadlift, single-leg squats) vs traditional resistance training
summary: This systematic review and meta-analysis of 7 RCTs (119 basketball players) found that flywheel resistance training produced moderate beneficial effects on jump performance (Hedges' g = 0.65) and change-of-direction performance (Hedges' g = -0.57) compared to traditional resistance training, while the effect on linear sprint performance (Hedges' g = -0.57) did not reach statistical significance.
key_findings: Jump performance favored flywheel training with a moderate effect (Hedges' g = 0.65, 95% CI [0.23, 1.07], p = 0.008) and negligible heterogeneity (I² = 0.0%).
Change-of-direction performance favored flywheel training with a moderate effect (Hedges' g = -0.57, 95% CI [-1.07, -0.08], p = 0.033) and no detected heterogeneity (I² = 0.0%).
Linear sprint performance showed a moderate point estimate favoring flywheel training (Hedges' g = -0.57, 95% CI [-1.20, 0.05]) but did not reach statistical significance (p = 0.065).
Evidence certainty was rated moderate for jump performance and low for sprint and COD performance per GRADE.
All 7 included studies had some concerns for risk of bias, primarily in randomization and outcome reporting.
limitations: Only 7 studies with small total sample (n=119) limited statistical power to detect heterogeneity; all studies had some risk-of-bias concerns (randomization, outcome reporting); GRADE certainty low for sprint and COD outcomes.
